## Overview
In the modern-day, resources consumption is increasing exponentially leading to mass depletion, pollution and overall, adverse impacts on the environment. As society begins to value sustainable practices, industries are forced to reevaluate resource usage. For the transportation industry, public transit is a safer, environmental friendly, alternative to driving for example. However, while an individual train ride has less effect than a personal car, many public transit agencies do not have green practices.\
\
This impact is measured by CO~2~ emissions. As defined by the [U.S. Energy Information Administration](https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/index.php?id=carbon%20intensity), carbon intensity refers to the “amount of carbon by weight emitted per unit of energy consumed”. In an emissions context, a higher carbon intensity means more CO~2~ emissions, which is not ideal for industries with significant energy consumption (like public transit).\
\
At Green Transit Alliance (GTA), we value green practices in the transportation industry. That is why annually, we recognize public transit agencies with the “greenest” outcomes. Our decisions are based on a comprehensive analysis of three federal sources which will be discussed in an upcoming section.\
\
Congratulations in advance to the winners!


## Data Acquisition
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)
library(httr2)
library(rvest)
library(skimr)
library(scales)
library(gt)
```
The data was acquired from two federal sources - the [National Transit Database](https://www.transit.dot.gov/ntd) and the [U.S. Energy Information Administration](https://www.eia.gov/).

### U.S. Energy Information Administration
#### State Electricity Profiles
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

get_eia_sep <- function(state, abbr){
    library(tidyverse)
    library(stringr)
    library(httr2)
    library(rvest)
    library(fs)
  
    state_formatted <- str_to_lower(state) |> str_replace_all("\\s", "")
    
    dir_name <- fs::path("data", "mp02")
    file_name <- fs::path(dir_name, state_formatted)
    
    fs::dir_create(dir_name, recurse=TRUE)
    
    if(!fs::file_exists(file_name)){
        BASE_URL <- "https://www.eia.gov"
        RESPONSE <- request(BASE_URL) |> 
          req_url_path("electricity", 
                       "state", 
                       state_formatted) |>
          req_headers(
            `User-Agent` = "Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10.15; rv:149.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/149.0"
            ) |>   
          req_retry(
                max_tries = 4, 
          ) |>
          req_perform(file_name)
    
        resp_check_status(RESPONSE)
    }
    
    TABLE <- read_html(file_name) |> 
        html_element("table") |> 
        html_table() |>
        mutate(Item = str_to_lower(Item))
    
    if("U.S. rank" %in% colnames(TABLE)){
        TABLE <- TABLE |> rename(Rank = `U.S. rank`)
    }
    
    CO2_MWh <- TABLE |> 
        filter(Item == "carbon dioxide (lbs/mwh)") |>
        pull(Value) |> 
        str_replace_all(",", "") |>
        as.numeric()
    
    PRIMARY <- TABLE |> 
        filter(Item == "primary energy source") |> 
        pull(Rank)
    
    RATE <- TABLE |>
        filter(Item == "average retail price (cents/kwh)") |>
        pull(Value) |>
        as.numeric()
    
    GENERATION_MWh <- TABLE |>
        filter(Item == "net generation (megawatthours)") |>
        pull(Value) |>
        str_replace_all(",", "") |>
        as.numeric()
    
    data.frame(CO2_MWh               = CO2_MWh, 
               primary_source        = PRIMARY,
               electricity_price_MWh = RATE * 10, # / 100 cents to dollars &
               # * 1000 kWh to MWH 
               generation_MWh        = GENERATION_MWh, 
               state                 = state, 
               abbreviation          = abbr
    )
}

EIA_SEP_REPORT <- map2(state.name, state.abb, get_eia_sep) |> list_rbind()
```

The US Energy Information Administration is a repository for energy data across the United States. For the purpose of this project, Green Transit Alliance is interested in the summaries for state electricity profiles. The code above does this, storing the result in a data frame titled `EIA_SEP_REPORT`.

Each entry represents one state with information regarding pounds of carbon dioxide emissions per megawatt hour, primary sources of electricity generation, average retail prices of electricity and total generation capacity. Eventually this data will be coupled with information on public transit agencies to understand different energy sources they use as a fraction of total electricity consumption at the state level.

It is likely some type of joining function will be used. The most probable option is `inner_join` which will match columns present across multiple data sets. While the NTD data will be discussed later on, state data will be available. Given such, `EIA_SEP_REPORT` will likely be joined on the `state` or `abbreviation` column to gain a state-level picture on usage of fuel/electricity and carbon emissions by public transit agencies. Filters used depend on the analysis being conducted but it is possible they will be used to compare carbon emissions and electricity across various states.

### National Transit Database
The National Transit Database (NTD) is a repository for publicly available data on the finances, operations and assets in American public transit systems. It is managed by the Federal Transportation Administration (FTA). For Green Transit Alliance, information regarding how public transit agencies consume fuel and the amount of electricity they use as well. The services provided by transit systems are of interest as well.

#### Energy Consumption
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false


load_ntd_energy <- function(){
  library(readxl)
  library(httr2)
  library(tidyverse)
  library(fs)
  
  # Create 'data/mp02' directory if not already present
  DATA_DIR <- fs::path("data", "mp02")
  fs::dir_create(DATA_DIR, recurse=TRUE)

  NTD_ENERGY_FILE <- fs::path(DATA_DIR, "2025_ntd_energy.xlsx")

  if(!fs::file_exists(NTD_ENERGY_FILE)){
    library(httr2)
  
    request("https://www.transit.dot.gov/") |>
      req_url_path("sites",
                   "fta.dot.gov",
                   "files",
                   "2026-09",
                   "2025 Energy Consumption_260806.xlsx") |> 
      req_headers(
        `User-Agent` = "Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10.15; rv:149.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/149.0") |> 
      req_perform(NTD_ENERGY_FILE)
  }
  
  if(file.info(NTD_ENERGY_FILE)$size < 1e4){
        cat("I was unable to download the NTD Energy File. Please try again.\n")
        stop("Download failed. Please delete the corrupted file by running `unlink('data/mp02/2025_ntd_energy.xlsx')` and try again.")
    }

  to_numeric_fill_0 <- function(x){
    x <- if_else(x == "-", NA, x)
    replace_na(as.numeric(x), 0)
  }

  read_excel(NTD_ENERGY_FILE) |> 
    select(-c(`Reporter Type`, 
              `Reporting Module`, 
              `Gallons of Other Fuel`, 
              `Other Fuel Description`)) |>
    mutate(across(-c(`Agency Name`, 
                     `Mode`,
                     `TOS`), 
                  to_numeric_fill_0)) |>
    group_by(`NTD ID`, `Mode`, `Agency Name`) |>
    summarize(across(where(is.numeric), sum), 
              .groups = "keep") |>
    mutate(ENERGY = sum(c_across(c(where(is.numeric))))) |>
    filter(ENERGY > 0) |>
    select(-ENERGY) |>
    ungroup()
}

NTD_ENERGY <- load_ntd_energy()
```

The code above forms the database `NTD_ENERGY` which contains information on different transit agencies, their locations, the types of fuel they consume and in what amounts, and the amount of electricity they use as well. Some of the fuel types reported include gasoline, kerosene, biodiesel, and hydrogen to name a few. The electricity usage is reported in two metrics  - electricity propulsion and battery usage. These two categories just draw on the distinction between how electricity is acquired. Another important part of this data is the `Mode` column which specifies how services in transit agencies are provided. While these are currently listed as two letter abbreviations, they will be recorded in a future step according to the NTD Reporting Policy Manual.

As previously mentioned with the EIA data, an `inner_join` is the most appropriate for this data. While the `NTD_ENERGY` energy contains many more entries on different public transit agencies (local, citywide, etc.), understanding their resources consumption as a part of overall state electricity consumption is important to understand which transit agencies are the greenest.

#### Transit Service Provided
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

load_ntd_service <- function(){
  library(httr2)
  library(tidyverse)
  library(fs)
  
  # Create 'data/mp02' directory if not already present
  DATA_DIR <- fs::path("data", "mp02")
  fs::dir_create(DATA_DIR, recurse=TRUE)

  NTD_SERVICE_FILE <- fs::path(DATA_DIR, "2025_ntd_service.csv")

  if(!fs::file_exists(NTD_SERVICE_FILE)){
    library(httr2)
  
    request("https://data.transportation.gov/resource/4fir-qbim.csv") |>
      req_url_query(`$query`=paste(
        "SELECT  `_5_digit_ntd_id` AS `NTD_ID`", 
        "`max_agency` AS `AGENCY`",
        "`max_reporter_type` AS `reporter_type`",
        "`max_organization_type` AS `organization_type`",
        "`max_city` AS `city`",
        "`max_state` AS `state`",
        "`mode`",
        "`type_of_service`",
        "`max_primary_uza_code` as `uza_code`",
        "`max_primary_uza_name` as `uza_name`",
        "`max_primary_uza_area_sq_miles` as `uza_sq_miles`",
        "`max_primary_uza_population` as `uza_population`",
        "`max_service_area_sq_miles` as `service_area_sq_miles`",
        "`max_service_area_population` as `service_area_population`",
        "`questionable_record` as `flagged_likely_inaccurate`",
        "`sum_unlinked_passenger_trips_upt` as `total_upt`",
        "`sum_passenger_miles` WHERE caseless_one_of(`report_year`, '2025') limit 50000", 
        sep=",")) |>
      req_headers(
        `User-Agent` = "Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10.15; rv:149.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/149.0") |> 
      req_perform(NTD_SERVICE_FILE)
  }
  
  if(file.info(NTD_SERVICE_FILE)$size < 1e4){
        cat("I was unable to download the NTD Service File. Please try again.\n")
        stop("Download failed. Please delete the corrupted file by running `unlink('data/mp02/2025_ntd_service.xlsx')` and try again.")
    }

  read_csv(NTD_SERVICE_FILE) |>
    mutate(flagged_likely_inaccurate = !is.na(flagged_likely_inaccurate))
}

NTD_SERVICE <- load_ntd_service()
```

The `NTD_SERVICE` data contains information on passenger trips across different transit services. Each entry corresponds to a different service by a specific agency. The transit services reported are the same `mode` column from the `NTD_ENERGY` data. Given such they will also have to be recoded.

However the focus here is on how different services are serving different areas across the United States. There are columns titled `uza_sqmiles`/`uza_population` and `service_area_sq_miles`/`service_area_population`.These metrics specify how different transit systems are serving the public and in which amounts. There are also columns that have flags for inaccurate data. It is highly likely we will omit these records in our analysis to ensure fair, accurate reporting. 

Lastly, two significant metrics reported in this data are `total_upt` and `sum_passenger_miles`. `total_upt` represents unlinked passenger trips which means that one trip regardless of how many transfers will count as one UPT. For example if you take two trains to reach a destination it still counts as one UPT because it is one trip in two segments. On the other hand, `sum_passenger_miles` reports the cumulative miles traveled by all passengers in that transit system by a specific mode of transit.

An initial understanding of the data was conducted using the `glimpse()` and `skim()` functions whose outputs are not included in the report. However this understanding is essential to conceptualize how different data reports connect and contribute to the broader picture of green public transit.

The main concern here was translating the `mode` column in the NTD_ENERGY and NTD_SERVICE data sets into something more readable. As stated previously, the `mode` columns are originally reported as two letter abbreviations whose full forms represent various transit services. To understand which transit services are reported, the list of distinct values for each dataset was pulled and each of those abbreviations was translated into its full form. The abbreviations are shown in the code above and can also be accessed through the [NTD Reporting Policy Manual](https://www.transit.dot.gov/ntd/2025-ntd-reporting-policy-manual). 

## Data Integration and Initial Exploration

### EIA State Electricity Profiles
#### Most Expensive Retail Electricity
**Which 5 states have the most expensive retail electricity?**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: 80%

# Filter out the five states with the highest electricity prices per megawatt-hour
EIA_SEP_REPORT |> slice_max(electricity_price_MWh, n=5) |>
  # Use reorder to have the bar in descending order
  ggplot(aes(reorder(state, -electricity_price_MWh),electricity_price_MWh)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = dollar(electricity_price_MWh)), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0,0.15))) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title= "States with the Most Expensive Retail Electricity",
       x= "State", 
       y = "Price per Megawatt-Hour ($)") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t=12)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r=12))
  )
```
**Hawaii has the most expensive retail electricity** at $380 per megawatt-hour. Following Hawaii, in order of descending price, are California, Connecticut, Rhode Island and Massachusetts.


#### 'Dirtiest' Electricity Mix
**Which 5 states have the ‘dirtiest’ electricity mix?**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Filter out the five states with the highest CO2 per megawatt-hour
EIA_SEP_REPORT |> slice_max(CO2_MWh, n=5) |> 
  # Select only the relevant, needed columns
  select(c("state", "CO2_MWh", "primary_source")) |> 
  gt() |>
  cols_align(align = "left", columns = "CO2_MWh") |>
  fmt_number(CO2_MWh, decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(state=md("**State**"),
             CO2_MWh = md("**CO~2~ Emissions (lbs/MWh)**"), 
             primary_source = md("**Primary Source**")) |> 
  tab_header(title="States with the 'Dirtiest' Electricity Mix")

```
The ‘dirtiest’ electricity mix is defined as having high carbon emissions. Therefore, in other words, this question asks which states have the highest CO~2~ emissions in pounds per megawatt-hour. **West Virginia has the 'dirtiest' electricity mix** at 1,912 pounds of CO~2~ per megawatt-hour. West Virginia is followed by Kentucky, Wyoming, Missouri and Hawaii in descending order. Notably, four of the top five states with the 'dirtiest' electricity mix use coal as their primary source.


#### Average Co~2~ per Megawatt-Hour
**On average, how many pounds of CO2 are emitted per MWh of electricity produced in the US?**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Set up variable to call on in inline code
us_CO2_emission = EIA_SEP_REPORT |>
  # Compute a weighted mean for total CO2 emissions as a fraction of total generation (both in mwH)
  # Use weighted mean over simple mean to ensure states with smaller/bigger consumption are accurately represented in average CO2 emissions
  summarise(CO2_avg = weighted.mean(CO2_MWh, generation_MWh, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(CO2_avg)

```

On average, **`r round(us_CO2_emission)` pounds** of CO~2~ are emitted per megawatt hour of electricity produced in the United States.


#### Rarest Primary Energy Sources in the US
**What are the three rarest primary energy sources in the US? What is the associated cost of electricity associated with each source and in what states are they used?**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Group by primary source
EIA_SEP_REPORT |> group_by(primary_source) |>
  # Summarize number of states in each group and compute the average electricity price across those states
  summarise(
    state_count = n_distinct(state), 
    states_use = toString(state),
    avg_price = mean(electricity_price_MWh)) |>
  # Pull the three sources where the least number of states are using them
  slice_min(state_count, n=3) |>
  mutate(avg_price = round(avg_price, 2)) |>
  gt() |>
    cols_label(primary_source=md("**Primary Source**"),
               states_use = md("**States Using this Source**"),
               state_count=md("**State Count**"),
               avg_price = md("**Average Electricity Price ($/MWh)**")) |> 
  tab_header(title="Rarest Primary Energy Sources in the US")
```
The rarest primary energy source in the US is **petroleum** and it is used by only one state that has an average electricity price of \$380 per megawatt hour. 

Both the second and third rarest primary sources are used by four states and they are hydroelectric and wind energy. Idaho, Oregon, Vermont, and Washington use hydroelectric energy with an average electricity price of \$122.90 per megawatt hour. 

Wind energy is used by Iowa, Kansas, New Mexico and South Dakota with an average price of \$101.50 per megawatt hour. Notably the rarest primary source, petroleum, is used by Hawaii which is also the state with the highest average electricity price across the country.


### NTD Energy Usage
#### Visualizing Fuel Usage
**Across all US public transit, visualize the amounts of each type of fuel used.**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

NTD_ENERGY |> 
  # Change data format so eventually data can be grouped by fuel type
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("Gallons"), names_to = "fuel_type", values_to = "gallons", names_prefix = "Gallons of ") |>
  group_by(fuel_type) |> 
  # Aggregate the amount of gallons used across individual fuel type groups
  summarise(total_gallons = sum(gallons, na.rm = TRUE)/1000000) |>
  # Omit any fuel types that were unused
  filter(total_gallons > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(total_gallons, reorder(fuel_type, total_gallons))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(total_gallons)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0,0.2))) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title= "Consumption by Fuel Type Across US Public Transit",
       x= "Consumption (in millions of gallons)", 
       y = "Fuel Type") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t=12)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r=12)))
  
```
The most consumed fuel type across US public transit is **diesel fuel at 437.93 million gallons**. Second to it is compressed natural gas but in terms of gallons consumed it is only 45.4% of diesel fuel at 198.83 million gallons. This is a massive difference and it is plausible that diesel fuel is the standard for fuel type used by transportation systems.

In third place is gasoline, but that value is half that of compressed natural gas usage. Following it are biodiesel, liquid petroleum gas, ethanol and lastly liquid natural gas, which is only about 220,000 gallons. 


#### Least Common Fuel Source for U.S. Public Transit
**What is the least commonly used fuel source for US public transit?**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Set up variable to call on in inline code
least_common = NTD_ENERGY |>
  # Change data format so eventually data can be grouped by fuel type
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("Gallons"), names_to = "fuel_type", values_to = "gallons", names_prefix = "Gallons of ") |>   
  group_by(fuel_type) |>
  # Aggregate the amount of gallons used across individual fuel type groups
  summarise(total_gallons = sum(gallons, na.rm = TRUE)) |>   
  # Omit any fuel types that were unused
  filter(total_gallons > 0) |> 
  # Find the fuel type with the lowest consumption
  slice_min(total_gallons) |> 
  # Extract the name of that fuel type
  pull("fuel_type")

```
The least commonly used fuel source for US public transit is **`r least_common`**. This conclusion is also available in the previous tasks where all fuel types were graphically compared.


### NTD Service
#### Transit Services with the Most Annual UPT
**Which five transit services have the most UPT annually?**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

top_5_upt_data = NTD_SERVICE |>
  # Remove all possible inaccurate entries
  filter(!flagged_likely_inaccurate) |>
  # Format agency name to only include name and omit unnecessary details
  mutate(AGENCY = str_remove(AGENCY, ", dba:.*")) |>
  # Group by agency and mode to figures out with agencies in what services have the most UPT
  group_by(AGENCY, mode) |>
  # Sum total upt across these groups
  summarise(upt = sum(total_upt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  # Add a column including the agency name and transit service for a UPT value
  mutate(service = paste0(AGENCY, " (", mode ,")")) |>
  # Extract top five UPTs
  slice_max(upt, n=5)

# Reorder service and UPT to show values in descending order
ggplot(top_5_upt_data, aes(x = upt, y = reorder(service, upt))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale_cut = cut_short_scale())(upt)),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 3.8
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 28)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Transit Services with the Most Annual UPT",
    x = "Total Unlinked Passenger Trips",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = 'plot',
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5
                              ),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```
**MTA New York City Transit holds the top two spots for transit services with the most annual UPT.** Heavy rails sits at the top with 2.3 billion UPTs annually with motorbus in second place at 661.5 million. 

Following MTA at number three is Los Angeles County’s Metropolitan motorbus transit service at 240 million UPTs. Next is Chicago Transit Authority’s motorbus service at about 200 million and at fifth is Washington D.C.’s  heavy rail system at about 180 million UPTs.

It is understandable that most of the five services with the highest UPTs are in population dense areas. It also makes sense that three of these spots are for motorbus services. While cities are expanding their heavy rail systems, they are still not as extensive as bus routes are. Logically, bus routes are more manageable and there is more flexibility in how they are designed/the places they reach.

One important data nuance to consider is how the NTD tracks UPTs across different transit services. For example, switching from a bus to a train is still considered a transfer in New York City. Does it count as two UPTs since they are different transit systems or because it is considered a transfer it is only one passenger trip? 


#### Average Trip Length for MTA New York City Transit 
**What is the average trip length of a trip on MTA NYC?**
``` {r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Set up variable to call on in inline code
avg_trip_length = NTD_SERVICE |> 
  # Remove all possible inaccurate entries
  # Only keep entries that have "MTA New York City Transit" in the agency name
  filter(!flagged_likely_inaccurate, str_detect(AGENCY, "MTA New York City Transit")) |>
  # Divide sum of passenger miles across the MTA by the total number of trips taken
  summarise(avg_trip = sum(sum_passenger_miles)/sum(total_upt)) |> 
  pull(avg_trip)

```
The average trip length for MTA New York City Transit is **`r round(avg_trip_length,2)` miles**.


#### Least Miles Traveled by Public Transit
**Which five states has the fewest total miles traveled by public transit?**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Remove all possible inaccurate entries
NTD_SERVICE |> filter(!flagged_likely_inaccurate) |>
  # Only include states by using built in 'state.abb' (no territories and other regions)
  filter(state %in% state.abb) |>
  group_by(state) |>
  # Across each state, sum total passenger miles
  # Divide by 1 million to make graphical reporting easier
  summarise(tot_miles = sum(sum_passenger_miles, na.rm = TRUE)/1000000) |>
  filter(tot_miles > 0) |>
  # Extract the five states with the fewest total miles traveled
  slice_min(tot_miles, n = 5) |>
  # Add a column with the full state name since original data only contained abbreviations
  mutate(full_state = set_names(state.name, state.abb)[state]) |>
  # Reorder states to show in acsending order
  ggplot(aes(tot_miles, reorder(full_state, -tot_miles))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(tot_miles)), hjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0,0.5))) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title= "States with Fewest Total Miles Travelled by Public Transit",
       x= "Total Miles Traveled by Public Transit (in millions)",
       y = NULL) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t=12)))
```
**South Dakota** has the fewest total miles traveled by public transit at 2.31 million miles. Following South Dakota, is New Hampshire, North Dakota, Mississippi, and Idaho in that order.

Something worth noting is that originally, the state with the fewest total miles by public transit was Wyoming at zero. This was a confusing metric because looking at Wyoming‘s records they did have entries for everything else except total passenger miles. Upon further investigation, it was discovered that the FTA has different reporting regulations for agencies according to their size. The two levels are ‘full reporter’ and ‘reduced reporter’. While it is not known why Wyoming did not report these metrics, we can assume that it may be a personal choice to not include passenger miles.

``` {r}

upt_nuclear = NTD_SERVICE |>
```

There were **`r comma(upt_nuclear)`** unlinked passenger trips recorded where the primary energy source was nuclear power.

``` {r}
               mutate(join_id = as.integer(NTD_ID)) |>
```

## Data Analysis
### Calculate Total Emissions
Compute the total emissions associated with each Agency + Mode pair.
``` {r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Subset EIA data to include only state abbreviation and CO2 per megawatt hour columns
grid_intensity = EIA_SEP_REPORT |> 
  select(abbreviation, grid_CO2 = CO2_MWh)

energy_mode = NTD_ENERGY |> 
  # Add column with ntd id as an integer (both NTD datasets have different ways of reporting ID)
  mutate(join_id = as.integer(`NTD ID`)) |> 
  # Create groups for the same agencies with the same transit services 
  group_by(join_id, Mode) |> 
  # Sum fuel consumption by individual fuel type across transit services
  summarise(
    diesel_gal    = sum(`Gallons of Diesel Fuel`, na.rm = TRUE),
    biodiesel_gal = sum(`Gallons of Bio-Diesel`, na.rm = TRUE),
    gasoline_gal  = sum(`Gallons of Gasoline`, na.rm = TRUE),
    cng_gal       = sum(`Gallons of Compressed Natural Gas`, na.rm = TRUE),
    lng_gal       = sum(`Gallons of Liquified Nat Gas`, na.rm = TRUE),
    lpg_gal       = sum(`Gallons of Liquified Petroleum Gas`, na.rm = TRUE),
    bunker_gal    = sum(`Gallons of Bunker Fuel`, na.rm = TRUE),
    kerosene_gal  = sum(`Gallons of Kerosene`, na.rm = TRUE),
    ethanol_gal   = sum(`Gallons of Ethanol`, na.rm = TRUE),
    electric_kwh  = sum(`Kilowatt hours of Electric Propulsion`, na.rm = TRUE) + 
                    sum(`Kilowatt hours of Electric Battery`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

agencymode_emissions = NTD_SERVICE |>
  # Remove all possible inaccurate entries
  filter(!flagged_likely_inaccurate) |> 
  # Add column with ntd id as an integer (both NTD datasets have different ways of reporting ID)
  mutate(join_id = as.integer(NTD_ID)) |> 
  # Group by following columns
  # Include both join_id and agency so they appear as separate columns
  group_by(join_id, AGENCY, state, mode) |> 
  # Sum total UPT and passenger miles across agency + mode
  summarise(
    tot_upt = sum(total_upt, na.rm = TRUE),
    tot_pmt = sum(sum_passenger_miles, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 
  # Join emissions with energy mode data on the join_id and mode/Mode columns
  # Use inner join to keep entries with only both service and energy data
  inner_join(energy_mode, by = join_by(join_id == join_id, mode == Mode)) |> 
  # Use a left join to match records by state
  left_join(grid_intensity, by = join_by(state == abbreviation)) |>
  # Add a column to compute the emissions for each fuel type
  mutate(
    em_diesel   = diesel_gal * 22.45,
    em_bio      = biodiesel_gal * (9.45*2.2046),
    em_gasoline = gasoline_gal * 18.73,
    em_cng      = cng_gal * (120.85/10),
    em_lng      = lng_gal * (4.50*2.2046),
    em_lpg      = lpg_gal * 12.68,
    em_bunker   = bunker_gal * (11.27*2.2046),
    em_kerosene = kerosene_gal * 21.78,
    em_ethanol  = ethanol_gal * (5.75*2.2046),
    # Compute carbon emission by converting to mwh and multiplying by carbon intensity by state
    em_electric = (electric_kwh / 1000) * grid_CO2,
    total_emissions_lbs = em_diesel + em_bio + em_gasoline + em_cng + 
                          em_lng + em_lpg + em_bunker + em_kerosene + 
                          em_ethanol + em_electric
  )

```

### Relate Total Emissions and Passenger Service
Normalizing total emissions for each Agency + Mode pair by the actual size of the transit agency.
``` {r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false


agency_efficiency = agencymode_emissions |> 
  group_by(join_id, AGENCY, state) |> 
  summarise(
    total_emissions_lbs = sum(total_emissions_lbs, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_upt           = sum(tot_upt, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_pmt           = sum(tot_pmt, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 
  filter(total_upt > 0, total_pmt > 0) |> 
  mutate(
    per_upt = total_emissions_lbs / total_upt,
    per_pmt = total_emissions_lbs / total_pmt,
    agency_size = case_when(
      total_upt >= 50e6 ~ "Large",
      total_upt >= 5e6  ~ "Medium",
      TRUE              ~ "Small"
    )
  )

# Best efficiency by agency size and per UPT
agency_efficiency |> 
  filter(state %in% state.abb) |>
  group_by(agency_size) |> 
  slice_min(per_upt, n = 1) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  select(agency_size, AGENCY, state, per_upt, total_upt) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = per_upt, decimals = 3) |> 
  fmt_number(columns = total_upt, decimals = 0) |> 
  cols_label(
    agency_size = md("**Agency Size**"),
    AGENCY      = md("**Transit Agency**"),
    state       = md("**State**"),
    per_upt     = md("**CO~2~ Emissions (lbs/UPT)**"),
    total_upt   = md("**Total Trips (UPT)**")
  ) |> 
  tab_header(
    title    = "Greenest Transit Agencies",
    subtitle = "by unlinked passenger trips")

# Best efficiency by agency size and per passenger mile traveled
agency_efficiency |> 
  filter(state %in% state.abb) |>
  group_by(agency_size) |> 
  slice_min(per_pmt, n = 1) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  select(agency_size, AGENCY, state, per_pmt, total_pmt) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = per_pmt, decimals = 3) |> 
  fmt_number(columns = total_pmt, decimals = 0) |> 
  cols_label(
    agency_size = md("**Agency Size**"),
    AGENCY      = md("**Transit Agency**"),
    state       = md("**State**"),
    per_pmt     = md("**CO~2~ Emissions (lbs/PMT)**"),
    total_pmt   = md("**Total Passenger Miles**")
  ) |> 
  tab_header(
    title    = "Greenest Transit Agencies",
    subtitle = "by passgenger miles traveled")
```

Across unlinked passenger trips and passenger miles traveled the results for the greenest transit agencies were the same.

- **Large**: Tri-County Metropolitan Transportation District of Oregon\
For unlinked passenger trips, the TriMet system was emitting about 0.4 pounds of carbon per UPT out of 65.6 million total trips . By passenger miles traveled, the TriMet system had 0.097 pounds of carbon emissions per unit out of almost 270 million total passenger miles.
- **Medium**: Anaheim Transportation Network\
For unlinked passenger trips, Anaheim Regional Transportation was emitting about 0.126 pounds of carbon per UPT out of 8.2 million total trips . By passenger miles traveled, Anaheim Regional Transportation had 0.09 pounds of carbon emissions per unit out of almost 11.5 million total passenger miles.
- **Small**: City of Seattle\
For unlinked passenger trips, the Seattle Center Monorail  was emitting about 0.058 pounds of carbon per UPT out of 2.29 million total trips . By passenger miles traveled, the Seattle Center Monorail  had 0.064 pounds of carbon emissions per unit out of almost 2.06 million total passenger miles.
